one_liner: C library for SIMD binary packing of 128-integer blocks (SIMD-BP128); decodes several times faster than Simple-8b and scalar VByte.
what_it_does: Packs blocks of 128 unsigned 32-bit integers into b 128-bit words, where b is the block's maximum bit width, and unpacks them again; variants handle sorted lists with fused delta coding (simdpackd1/simdunpackd1), frame-of-reference (simdpackFOR), arbitrary lengths (simdpack_length, *_shortlength), and in-place select, search and set on packed blocks. It is deliberately low level: it defines no container format, so the caller must store each block's bit width, the initial delta offset and the element count.
how_it_is_fast: SIMD-BP128 (Lemire and Boytsov, 'Decoding billions of integers per second through vectorization', SPE 2015) lays integers out vertically across the four 32-bit lanes of an SSE register, so 4 values are shifted, masked and ORed per instruction with no per-value branches. There is one fully unrolled pack/unpack kernel per bit width 0-32 selected by a switch, and the d1 variants fuse the delta prefix sum into the unpack. AVX2 (256-integer) and AVX-512 (512-integer) kernels exist when compiled with those ISAs, and a small in-tree NEON shim maps the SSE intrinsics on AArch64.
when_to_use: Large arrays of small or slowly growing 32-bit integers (posting lists, column chunks, sorted docids) where decode throughput matters more than squeezing the last bits.
Sorted lists that need delta decode plus fast lower-bound search or select inside a packed block without fully unpacking (simdsearchd1, simdselectd1).
Building your own compressed format or index (as upscaledb, EventQL and ManticoreSearch do) where you want permissively licensed (BSD-3-Clause) kernels instead of a GPL codec.
x86-64 with SSE4.1 or better, or AArch64 with NEON, and data lengths that are mostly multiples of 128.
when_not_to_use: Skewed data with occasional large outliers: one big value sets the bit width for the whole 128-block; on gov2 it stores 21.8% of raw size vs 18.9% for Simple-8b and about 14% for PFor-style codecs (TurboPFor, OptPFD) in the TurboPFor table.
Short arrays (under 128 values): the *_shortlength paths are documented as much slower; LittleIntPacker targets that case.
64-bit integers: the API is 32-bit only (issue #34 asks about uint64_t and is open).

Untrusted compressed input: there is no format and no validation; a libFuzzer heap-buffer-overflow report (issue #21, 2018) is closed without a visible fix, and the bit width and length come from the caller.
If the fastest decode is all that matters and GPL is acceptable, TurboPFor's TurboPackV256 beats it in the same gov2 table (11902 vs 9488 MB/s decode, 14466 vs 6952 MB/s encode).

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (CMake target simdcomp::simdcomp, pkg-config file, FetchContent supported)
integration.dependencies: none for the library; the optional benchmarks fetch lemire/counters over the network and need C++17
integration.min_toolchain: C89/C90 compiler with extensions (GCC, Clang, MSVC); CMake 3.14
integration.platforms: x86/x86-64 (SSE2 for core packing, SSE4.1 for some helpers, optional AVX2/AVX-512 kernels); AArch64/ARM NEON via include/neon128.h (added June 2026)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; functions are stateless and operate on caller buffers

gotchas: The CMake option SIMDCOMP_NATIVE defaults to ON and compiles with -march=native, so a library built on one machine may crash with illegal instructions on an older CPU; set -DSIMDCOMP_NATIVE=OFF for distributed binaries.

The AVX2 and AVX-512 functions (avxpack/avxunpack, avx512pack/avx512unpack) are only declared when the build enables those ISAs, use 256/512-integer blocks and produce a different layout from the 128-integer SSE format; do not mix them.

simdpackwithoutmask and simdpackwithoutmaskd1 assume every value (or delta) fits in b bits; an oversized value silently corrupts its neighbors. simdunpack with a bit width above 32 silently writes nothing.
The interleaved 4-lane layout is not the same as scalar sequential bit packing, so other libraries can read it only if they implement the same layout (the Rust bitpacking crate is a port).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose simdcomp over FastPFor or SIMDCompressionAndIntersection when you want a small C library with just the bit-packing kernels and your own block format; choose those C++ libraries for complete codecs with PFor exception handling (better ratio on skewed data) or list intersection. Over TurboPFor, pick it for the BSD license; over Stream VByte or MaskedVByte, pick it when data is blockable and you want both faster decode and smaller output.
verified_claims_summary: In the TurboPFor README gov2.sorted table (dated 2019.11, block 128 with delta coding, run by the TurboPFor author; issue #47 names a Skylake i7-6700 3.4 GHz and gcc 9.2 but no flags), SC_SIMDPack128 encoded at 6952 MB/s and decoded at 9488 MB/s vs Simple-8b 836/3296 and FastPFor's scalar VByte 1888/1980, while storing 21.8% of raw size vs 18.9% and 28.0%. The README's own claims (4 billion integers/s, 0.3 cycles per integer on Skylake) compare only against gzip, LZO, Snappy and LZ4 and come with no published run.
status_note: Mature (2019-2023 commits are mostly README and warning fixes) and still maintained by Daniel Lemire in the fast-pack org, with a CMake package and NEON support added on 2026-06-07; BSD-3-Clause and easy to vendor.
